title: Inside BMW's AI Gateway: Self-Hosting Cost-Efficient AI at Enterprise Scale | BMW | Ray Summit 2026

Um there's several advantages to this from

traceability, cost tracking, and even economy of scale effects um if you use a

applications of this gateway um yeah are quite limited, I would say. It's the

Of course, there's a lot of limitations to this offering. There's no

That's why we decided to basically add multimodality in 2025.
Now, the models here became a lot more capable.
We had, for example, the GPT-4 Vision model that understood vision as an
input. We have added text-to-speech and
speech-to-text capabilities with the speech and transcription endpoints.
And we even have generative offerings with an image generation and video

Of course, the applications now get extended, um for example, to speech
assistants and also other infotainment use cases that we're currently running
on our platform. While we made quite a step forward in
terms of the functionality, as you can see, we have a lot of um endpoints
available. In terms of a non-functional
perspective, we saw some limitations. First and foremost, uh there's a big
lock-in effect to vendors, but even to models.
A popular example for this is the Sora model, which um I believe many of you
would be familiar with. It's the basically the video generation model
developed by OpenAI, and it has recently been fully deprecated by them.
So, if you were relying on this model, you can no longer use it anymore.
We also saw limitations in the domain of data privacy, as with this approach,
your data will always leave your corporate network as it goes to the
hyperscaler. Lastly, the token cost, as we scale more
adoption and usage, is also a concern. We will see it later in this talk.
That's why we made the very conscious decision in 2026 to add self-hosting
capabilities to our AI gateway. What we're basically doing is we're
hosting Hugging Face open source models uh with KubeRay and vLLM on AWS EKS. So,
using Ray on on Kubernetes with KubeRay and using vLLM as the inference engine.
With this, we are able to serve popular models like the current free family or
also DeepSeek-V1. The application in this case, of course,
get extended. You can cover use cases where the data privacy is important.
Secondly, high-load use cases now make a lot of sense, because for those, you
might not want to pay per token, because the cost can scale quite a lot.
However, we saw some limitations with this approach still.
As you might know, with current Ray and vLLM, you can only um basically host
autoregressive models. Endpoints like image generation and
video generation usually rely on other architectures like diffusion models.
To fill this gap, I would like to make a quick excursion to vLLM Omni.
vLLM Omni is basically um an extension to vLLM for Omni modality
serving, which basically just means you can
provide multimodal inputs and also outputs.
It also supports non-autoregressive architectures like stable diffusion and
diffusion models. It's quite a new project still. It was
just released in November of 2025. Um it integrates natively with vLLM and it's
fully OpenAI compatible. That's why it's a perfect fit um to fill this gap
and it completes the phase four, which is the current stage of our AI gateway.
And it also completes the second part of our vision, which is of one gateway for
all. What do you see on the slide here? With
the addition of vLLM Omni, we achieve a full end-to-end multimodality, which
basically means for every of every of these endpoints, we're able to offer
self-hosted alternatives to the public cloud providers.
This is really quite amazing because it gives us a lot of added flexibility
deciding between self-hosting and managed APIs where it makes sense.
We can even go as far as doing intelligent load balancing between the
two. The applications here now get extended
further. Um you could think of things like multimodal personal content
generation, which is a field a lot of engineers are currently working at BMW.
Think of it at dynamically generating content based um on the current drive
that you're doing using image and video generation models.
Of course, high-load use cases like coding are still in scope.
Now, let me take you behind the scenes of how we're achieving this final phase
four of our AI gateway using also Ray. On a high level, if you start on the
left side, the request basically comes in from either the user or the vehicle.
Goes through a central DNS and will then reach our API gateway, which not only
exposes the AI gateway, but all of our other offerings.
The API gateway will then contact an identity provider to make sure that the
request is authenticated and also authorized.
Once the request is authenticated, uh we go to a model router, which in this case
is the light LLM proxy, which is a quite a popular open-source choice.
We can route to either Amazon Bedrock or Azure AI as our hyperscaler choices, or
even route to our own Ray internal service uh that of course is serving
open-source models. From a platform perspective, it's quite
important to us that we are centrally collecting all of the um metrics uh
with an OpenTelemetry collector, so metrics, logs, and traces from every
component get centrally collected and can be visualized in Grafana for our
platform monitoring, for system metrics, for example, and also on LangFuse, which
is a very popular AI observability platform for the application monitoring,
so for the actual use case monitoring. Let's go one level deeper and take a
look at our Ray setup. Once again, let's start with the request
entering through our light LLM proxy.
It can then be routed to our central Ray head, which is serving the Ray service.
The Ray service is then communicating with the different models that are of
course hosted on different GPU workers. In this case, we have a vLLM worker,
which is running natively vLLM and can serve chat models like GLM 5.2, MiniMax,
and 2.7, and the Qwen 3.6 as an example. If you need image or video generation
models, we can go through the vLLM Omni worker group, which runs the added
extension of vLLM Omni, and we can serve models like VAE 2.2 for video or Flux 2
for image generation. On the model storage layer, I would like
to add of course we're using Hugging Face as our model hub, and we're also
adding EFS as a caching layer to reduce uh the loading times during startup.
From an infrastructure perspective, as I already mentioned, we're running um
basically AWS EKS with the Kuber operator and also Carpenter for dynamic
uh scheduling and scaling of GPU nodes and also CPU nodes.
Lastly, of course, the observability is still very important on the left-hand
side, and we can collect metrics even down to an engine level from vLLM.
Let's take a look at the actual code um of our Ray service and basically how we
decided to implement this. What were the design goals here for this
implementation? We wanted to achieve a maximum model coverage.
What I mean by this is we wanted to basically support
the most model architect- architectures that we could and basically support the
most use cases without having to maintain a ton of different like um
inference engines or runtimes or even Docker images. This is why Ray and vLLM
are perfect choices because out of the box they support a number of different
architectures. In addition, in terms of the cost, we
would like to achieve a very low idle cost but be scalable um if we need to.
You can see the current models that we are running on our Ray service on the
right-hand side. You can see the vLLM application that is
using um the native build OpenAI app to host the models like GLM 5.2, MiniMax,
and also Qwen. For the uh vLLM Omni models, we have, as
I mentioned, the Flux 2 and the One model hosted.
Going to the hardware setup on EKS, uh we have provisioning and dynamic scaling
with Carpenter, which is quite important to us.
And in addition, I would like to mention uh that we the main workloads basically
are currently operating in EU Central 1, which comes with quite a lot of GPU
limitations. So, the popular H200, B200 cards that
you used to for LLM serving are not available there. So, we need to look
also for alternatives, as we will see. Lastly, why did we decide for one Ray
service for all of those models? I think it has several advantages. We can do
shared scaling and and scheduling on GPUs. The example for
this could be to use one large GPU that serves several replicas of a model of
smaller models and they can share them efficiently and with this we achieve a
high GPU utilization. Also, the routing is quite simple
because Light LLM just routes to one ray service which internally then routes to
the different models.
If you need special dependencies like in the vLLM Omni case, you can basically
use the dedicated GPU worker groups which we will now dive
deep into. First and foremost, for the Qwen 3.6
serving of a MiniMax, we're using native vLLM and the image provided by Ray with
the version 256. We're serving this on an Nvidia RTX 6000
card which has 96 GB of VRAM. This enabler enables us actually to use
the 4-bit quantization weights which you like saves quite a bit of GPU VRAM.
We can see on the right-hand side on the top that we're serving Qwen 3.6
some of them on one GPU in this case as you can see in the screenshot from the
Ray dashboard. Some optimizations that we are doing is
speculative decoding and we can also see that this is a multi-model model with
image and video endpoint input.
Let's talk about the MiniMax model quickly. We use two We have to use two
RTX Pro Blackwell cards in this case and even to make the model fit on it, we

make this fit barely on the two GPUs. Let me continue with the largest serving
that we're currently running in production which is the GLM 5.2 model.
We're starting off with the native Ray LLM 256 image, but we have to do some
manual adjustments. We have to update the VLLM
version to a more up-to-date version to up the basically support this GLM
architecture and also update a CUDA. In addition, there are some manual
patches that you have to do to support the RTX Pro architecture, which is
basically the SM120 architecture internally.

is really good for us. In terms of the model itself, the GLM
5.2 is a model with 743 billion parameters. It's a mixture of expert

In its full precision, it's basically 1.6 terabyte of weights. Of course, we
again running the 4-bit quantization weights from Nvidia.

right here. And for a model this size, it does make
sense to you to direct GPU weight loading with Run:AI stream in this case.
So basically skipping the CPU and loading the weights directly to the GPU.
For performance, it also helps to do KB cache over routing, which Ray also
supports.
Now, let me quickly walk you through the results of the connected app from
Gateway. For this talk, we would like to focus on
how we can save costs with this approach. And the use case that I picked
for today is agentic coding. Now, what is the goal in detail? We
would like to reduce agentic coding costs by replacing frontier APIs with

us? Coding assistants in the industry are
largely moving away from flat subscription fees to usage-based
pricing. This completely changes the economy of
AI coding as the costs directly scale now with usage.

really here an investment for the future that will pay off.

for the Qwen 3.6, we can see
that all of those models still maintain a usable threshold of roughly

support at least 16, so our pilot is basically ready to go. It can support
our user base.

So, what this means is for us that for this pilot the business case is

cost savings. Now, this pilot is already running for
roughly a month and the real world data actually also this theoretical

the Opus model class. And we believe that the savings will
scale with more usage and adoption, which is why we have decided to extend

Let me quickly wrap up the results and give an outlook for the future.
So, in terms of results, I think we have shown that we are providing BMW with a
scalable multi-model AI gateway and we're serving millions of requests per
month already in production. Now, with the hosting with Ray and vLLM,
we're adding flexibility and also data privacy to this AI gateway.
We have even shown there's substantial cost savings to be made when you're

that BMW benefits from our AI gateway. Some lessons learned along the way. So,

Specifically, we have, for example, identified a GPU shortage in Europe.

We have identified that the performance tuning for in vLLM and Ray, uh it's
mostly done on a per model basis. There's not really a one-size-fits-all

error involved. Same goes if you want to host the most
up-to-date and latest open source models, things like GLM and Kimmy.
Sometimes it requires some manual engineering or patching as we have seen
because of course VLLM and Ray cannot always
on day one support those architectures. Overall, we can summarize that efficient

Let me give you a quick outlook to the future for this topic.
We personally believe that the gap between frontier and open source models

adoption on our platform. So, we as a connected app platform
believe that hosting is still the way to go in 2026 and beyond even for like
non-tech enterprises like BMW because we get enabled by Ray and VLLM.
Thank you very much for your attention. This has been my talk and I can take
